abstract: Cutaneous scarring spans regenerative and normal remodelling; keloid, hypertrophic, atrophic and contractile outcomes; dyspigmentation; radiation- and inherited-fragility-associated fibrosis; and rare malignant transformation. Diagnostic labels alone do not capture the molecular, cellular, spatial and clinical states that shape these outcomes. This review is the first to treat the whole cutaneous scar spectrum, rather than keloid and hypertrophic scar alone, as a single computable phenotype space, and to audit jointly the provenance of the underlying datasets and the depth of validation of the resulting models. We searched four sources (PubMed, Europe PMC, OpenAlex and Crossref) on 20 June 2026 and combined systematic searching with evidence mapping; 26,575 records were identified, 920 entered the evidence map and 120 were prioritised for synthesis. Bulk studies identify tissue-level fibrotic programmes, whereas single-cell and spatial approaches resolve fibroblast, immune, endothelial and epithelial states and niches. Evidence remains concentrated in keloid and hypertrophic scar, and often reuses public datasets or extrapolates from associated cutaneous-fibrosis systems. Atrophic scars are represented mainly by quantitative imaging and treatment studies: topography and dermal loss are measurable, but no mature molecular or spatial atlas is available and atrophic acne scars are usually excluded from molecular cohorts. Scar pigmentation lacks interoperable labels, calibrated colour measurement, melanocyte-resolved spatial resources and skin-tone-stratified assessment. Fourteen studies applied artificial intelligence directly to scar data, but only one explicitly reported independent external validation. Molecular biomarkers and treatment-response models remain at discovery or internal-validation stages. Future work should standardise multidimensional phenotypes, build prospective skin-tone-stratified cohorts across the full scar spectrum, resolve rare populations such as melanocytes, and complete causal and external validation before clinical deployment.

New ZealandClin Cosmet Investig Dermatol1015434491178-7015Scars are not one condition. A burn, a surgical incision, trauma or acne can heal into a flat mature scar, a raised keloid or hypertrophic scar, a sunken atrophic scar, a tight contracture, or an area of changed skin colour. Most laboratory research on scars has studied keloids and raised scars, so the other scar types are much less well understood, and treatments still depend mainly on scar type, site and clinical experience. New laboratory and computer methods are changing this. Sequencing single cells, mapping molecules within tissue slices, and measuring scars with cameras, ultrasound and stiffness devices can describe a scar in far more detail than a clinical photograph, and artificial intelligence can use these measurements to predict how a scar may behave. These tools help only if scars are described in the same way, if the measurements are calibrated, and if the results hold up in new patients. This review maps the available evidence across the whole scar spectrum. It shows that molecular studies still concentrate on keloids and raised scars, that atrophic scars are studied mainly by imaging, and that changes in scar colour are measured inconsistently. Of the 14 studies that applied artificial intelligence to scar data, only one tested its model on independent data.
